source_text: Existimo ego sollicitum lectorem posse mirari, cur cum opusculum meum certo librorum numero, ex scribentium sollemnitate distinxerim, tamen libri alterius solvam in altero quaestiones; unde est illud quod in tertio volumine disputavi, Apostoli sensus, qui per unum hominem peccatum in mundo intrasse dixit [n1] (quo numero opinionem mali originalis oppressit), illud quod ex uno Abraham generatio Iudaeorum descendisse perhibetur [n2] , nihil vel exigui intulisse concussus. Id autem putet lector iste, cui nunc satisfacere instituo, in secundo debuisse volumine collocari. Norit igitur, hanc responsionis fidem, qua etiam illa quae putantur intermissa, vel in libro sequenti supplentur, nec quidquam incommodare certamini, nec de ulla festinationis perturbatione, sed tam de causarum necessitate, quam de consilii ratione contingere. Suppetit vero magnorum ingeniorum copia, quorum exemplis talis stili consequentia vindicetur; sed inepta iactatio est, ad defensionem simplicis negotii sonantia priscorum nominum advocare suffragia, et securitatem facti reddere defensione suspectam. Secundum ergo librum, quem asserendis Apostoli sententiis destinaram, ne in nimiam longitudinem levium quaestionum proferret adiectio, disputatione necessaria terminavi. Verum quia munere seriae dissertationis impleto, libuit etiam ineptis quaestionibus obviare, et tardissimorum quorumque, qui et frigidis possunt obiectionibus permoveri, placuit habere respectum, tertio libro qualiter ex uno multi nati dicerentur ostendi. Est tamen etiam decentissimum, si volumen sequens prioris debitum luat, ut et magna inter libros videatur esse concordia, et ad cognitionem totius operis invitentur legentes; cum et si dilata in primis aliqua aestimaverint, intellegunt praetermissa non esse. Ostenso igitur fidei et industriae operis convenire quod fecimus, congrediamur cum Manichaeis pro Dei operibus et legibus; ab illis naturalis mali deformitatem, ab istis iniquitatem iudiciorum feralium repellentes; docentes in istarum praeceptis nihil de bono suo perdidisse iustitiam, in illorum seminibus nihil de malo suo diabolum miscuisse; haec postremo digna esse Deo rectore, illa Deo dignissima conditore.
pass_a_gloss: I think an anxious reader can wonder why, although I have distinguished my little work by a definite number of books from the custom of writers, I nevertheless resolve the questions of one book in another; whence is that which I argued in the third volume, that the Apostle's sense, who said that through one man sin entered into the world (by which number he crushed the opinion of original evil), received no shaking even slight from that report that the generation of the Jews descended from one Abraham. But let that reader, whom I now set out to satisfy, think this ought to have been placed in the second volume. Let him know therefore that this faithfulness of reply, by which even those things which are thought omitted are supplied even in the following book, neither disadvantages the contest at all, nor happens from any disturbance of haste, but as much from the necessity of the causes as from the reason of a plan. There is indeed a supply of great talents, by whose examples such a sequence of style may be vindicated; but it is foolish boasting to call in the resounding suffrages of ancient names for the defense of a simple business, and to render the security of a deed suspect by defending it. Therefore the second book, which I had destined for asserting the Apostle's sentences, I terminated by the necessary disputation, lest the addition of light questions should carry it into excessive length. But because, the office of serious dissertation having been fulfilled, it pleased me also to meet foolish questions, and it pleased me to have regard for the slowest of people, who can be moved even by cold objections, I showed in the third book how from one many were said to have been born. Yet it is also most fitting if a following volume pays the debt of the earlier, so that both a great concord may be seen among the books, and readers may be invited to knowledge of the whole work; since even if they have judged some things postponed in the first, they understand they have not been omitted. Therefore, it having been shown that what we have done suits the faithfulness and industry of the work, let us join battle with the Manichaeans on behalf of God's works and laws; from the former driving back the ugliness of natural evil, from the latter the injustice of deadly judgments; teaching that in the precepts of the latter justice has lost nothing of its good, that in the seeds of the former the devil has mixed nothing of his evil; that these last are worthy of God as ruler, those most worthy of God as founder.

pass_b_english: I think an attentive reader may wonder why, although I have divided my little work into a definite number of books, as writers customarily do, I nevertheless settle in one book questions belonging to another. For example, in the third volume I argued that the statement that the Jewish people descended from the one man Abraham (Hebrews 11:12) did not in the slightest shake the apostle’s meaning when he said that sin entered the world through one man (Romans 5:12), a numerical expression that demolished the opinion of original evil. The reader whom I now intend to satisfy may think this should have been placed in the second volume. Let him understand, then, that this faithfulness in replying, by which even things thought to have been passed over are supplied in the following book, causes no disadvantage to the contest. It comes not from confusion caused by haste, but both from the requirements of the subject and from a considered plan. Many great minds offer examples that could justify such a sequence of writing. But it is foolish boasting to call on the resounding names of ancient writers to defend a simple matter, and to make an innocent action look suspicious by defending it.

I therefore ended the second book, which I had devoted to defending the apostle’s statements, when the necessary discussion was complete, so that adding trivial questions would not stretch it to excessive length. But after fulfilling the duty of serious argument, I chose to answer even foolish questions and to take account of the very slowest readers, who can be disturbed even by feeble objections. Accordingly, in the third book I showed how many people could be said to have been born from one. It is also entirely fitting for a following volume to discharge the debt of its predecessor: the books then show a strong agreement with one another, and readers are encouraged to learn the whole work. Even if they consider that some points were postponed in the earlier books, they understand that they were not omitted. Having shown, then, that what we have done accords with the work’s faithfulness and care, let us fight the Manichaeans on behalf of God’s works and laws. From his works we repel the ugliness of natural evil; from his laws, the injustice of deadly judgments. We teach that in the commands of those laws justice has lost none of its goodness, and into the seeds of those works the devil has mixed none of his evil. In short, the laws are worthy of God as ruler, and the works supremely worthy of God as creator.

choices.why: Julian names the opinion of original evil (mali originalis) as what Rom 5:12's 'one man' crushed; keep his phrase, not a later original-sin system.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
